explanations.explanation: Jesus is plain about it: if you do your righteous acts to be seen by men, “…you will have no reward from your Father in heaven.” (Matthew 6:1) Zero, friend. That's like stamping out a whole batch and finding out the oven was never on. All that work, nothing coming out warm.

Double sounds great, friend, but that's not what Jesus says. If you do your righteous acts to be seen by men, “…you will have no reward from your Father in heaven.” (Matthew 6:1) No reward at all, so there's nothing there to double.

Smaller is a reasonable guess, friend, but that's not what Jesus says. He says if you do your righteous acts to be seen by men, “…you will have no reward from your Father in heaven.” (Matthew 6:1) It isn't a little reward or a shrunken one. It's none.

That's the reason Jesus gives. The hypocrites give “…to be honored by men.” (Matthew 6:2) The gift is for the needy, but the trumpet is for the crowd. I think that's the loudest way anyone has ever asked for a thank-you.
Jesus doesn't say that. He says the hypocrites sound the trumpet “…to be honored by men.” (Matthew 6:2) The text gives the trumpet one purpose, and it's pointed at the crowd, not at the needy.
Prayer is a different subject, friend. It doesn't show up until verse 5. The trumpet in verse 2 is about giving, and the hypocrites sound it “…to be honored by men.” (Matthew 6:2)

Secret it is. Jesus says not to let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, “…so that your giving may be in secret.” (Matthew 6:3-4) Quiet giving, no trumpet. It's the kind of gift where even your own other hand is left out of the loop.
Public is how the hypocrites do it, friend. They sound a trumpet in the synagogues and on the streets (Matthew 6:2). Jesus says the opposite for you: your giving is to be “in secret.” (Matthew 6:4)

Faith sounds like it belongs, I'll give you that. But the word in the verse is “secret.” Jesus says not to let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, “…so that your giving may be in secret.” (Matthew 6:3-4)
True. Jesus says, “And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.” (Matthew 6:4) No crowd, no trumpet, and He still sees it. The one who matters is watching.

It's actually true, friend. Jesus says, “And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you.” (Matthew 6:4) Secret giving gets seen by the Father, and He rewards it. Nothing about it goes unnoticed.

explanations.answer: In the synagogues and on street corners
explanations.explanation: That's the spot. The hypocrites love to pray “…standing in the synagogues and on the street corners to be seen by men.” (Matthew 6:5) Synagogues are where people gathered, and street corners are where people walk by. Either way, it's a place with an audience.

explanations.answer: In the temple courts and the marketplaces
explanations.explanation: Close in sound, but that's not what Jesus says. He says they love to pray “…standing in the synagogues and on the street corners to be seen by men.” (Matthew 6:5) Keep an eye on those exact places, friend.

explanations.answer: At the town wells and the city squares
explanations.explanation: Those sound like places with plenty of people, but they aren't the ones Jesus names. He says the hypocrites love to pray “…standing in the synagogues and on the street corners to be seen by men.” (Matthew 6:5) Wells and city squares are fair guesses, friend. The two places to hold onto are the synagogues and the street corners.

Right. Jesus says, “…go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen.” (Matthew 6:6) The hypocrites pray where people can see. You go where it's just you and the Father.

The temple isn't the place Jesus names here, friend. He says to “…go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen.” (Matthew 6:6) Picture it: door shut, nobody watching, just you and your Father.

A quiet hill sounds peaceful, friend, but it's not in this verse. Jesus says, “…go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen.” (Matthew 6:6) The text sends you to a room.
Not quite, friend. Jesus says to go into your inner room and “…shut your door…” (Matthew 6:6) The door gets closed, not propped open. Then you pray to your Father, who is unseen.

False is right. Jesus says, “…go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen.” (Matthew 6:6) The door gets shut. My mustache could probably manage that, but I'd want a practice run.

Words is the first one. Jesus says the pagans “…think that by their many words they will be heard.” (Matthew 6:7) Their thinking is that more words means being heard. Jesus tells His listeners not to be like them (Matthew 6:8).

Heard is the second one. The pagans “…think that by their many words they will be heard.” (Matthew 6:7) That's what they're counting on: more words, more chances of being heard. Jesus says not to be like them.

Gifts came up earlier in the passage, friend, when Jesus talked about giving to the needy. But this verse is about prayer. Jesus says the pagans “…think that by their many words they will be heard.” (Matthew 6:7) The word that fits the blank is “words.”
Saved is a big word, but it isn't what the verse says. Jesus says the pagans “…think that by their many words they will be heard.” (Matthew 6:7) The word that fits the blank is “heard.”
Tears aren't mentioned anywhere in this verse. Jesus says the pagans “…think that by their many words they will be heard.” (Matthew 6:7) The blanks are filled by “words” and “heard.”
It's the other way around, friend. Jesus says, “…your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.” (Matthew 6:8) He knows ahead of time. You still ask, but you're not telling Him news.

False is right. Jesus says, “…your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.” (Matthew 6:8) He knows before a single word is said. That's why Jesus says not to be like the pagans with their many words.
True. Jesus says to pray like this: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name.” (Matthew 6:9) It opens by talking straight to the Father. No long speech first, just a simple start.
It's true, friend. The prayer Jesus gives begins, “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name.” (Matthew 6:9) That's the first thing out of the gate. It opens by calling God Father.

Not quite, friend. The prayer says, “Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10) Earth is right there in the request. It asks for God's will to be done on earth as it is in heaven.
False is right. The prayer says, “…Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10) Earth is right there in the request, not left out. It asks for God's will here too.
That's the request: “Give us this day our daily bread.” (Matthew 6:11) The word is “daily,” and it's for this day. I can respect a prayer that doesn't ask for more than that.
A full storehouse sounds nice, I won't argue. But the prayer says, “Give us this day our daily bread.” (Matthew 6:11) It asks for what's needed for the day.
A great harvest is a lot to ask for, friend, and it isn't in the prayer. Jesus gives these words: “Give us this day our daily bread.” (Matthew 6:11) That's the request.
Forgive fits the first blank. The prayer says, “And forgive us our debts…” (Matthew 6:12) It's a request, asking God to forgive. The second blank has a different word, so watch that one.

Forgiven goes in the second blank. The prayer says, “…as we also have forgiven our debtors.” (Matthew 6:12) Same word family as the first blank, but this one is about what we've already done. Easy to mix up, so good eye.
Pay is about debts, so I see why you'd reach for it. But the word in the first blank is “forgive.” The prayer says, “And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.” (Matthew 6:12)
Punished isn't in the verse, friend. The prayer asks God to forgive us our debts, “…as we also have forgiven our debtors.” (Matthew 6:12) The word for the second blank is “forgiven.”
Warned isn't in this line. The prayer says, “And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.” (Matthew 6:12) The blanks are “forgive” and “forgiven.”
That's it. The prayer says, “And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.” (Matthew 6:13) That's the last request in the prayer. It's the final thing Jesus has us ask.

Enemies are a natural guess, friend, but this verse doesn't name them. The prayer says, “And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.” (Matthew 6:13) I get it, I spent years in a junk drawer and I still wanted to blame the rubber band. Jesus points the request at the evil one, not at the neighbor, the boss or anybody else.
Hard times aren't mentioned here. The prayer ends, “…but deliver us from the evil one.” (Matthew 6:13) That's the request, friend, word for word.

Jesus says the opposite, friend. “But if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours.” (Matthew 6:15) It's a serious line, and He says it plainly. That makes this statement false.

False is right. Jesus says, “But if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours.” (Matthew 6:15) The line right before it says the other side: if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you (Matthew 6:14). It's a heavy one, and Jesus doesn't soften it.
Men is right. The hypocrites “…disfigure their faces to show men they are fasting.” (Matthew 6:16) The sad face is for people watching. It's an audience thing again.
It's the other way around, friend. The hypocrites disfigure their faces “…to show men they are fasting.” (Matthew 6:16) Jesus says to fast so it's seen only by your Father (Matthew 6:18).

Priests, friend? I see why you'd reach for them, but they never walk into this verse. Jesus says the hypocrites “…disfigure their faces to show men they are fasting.” (Matthew 6:16) The whole show is for whoever happens to be watching, and the verse calls them “men.” Picture a guy sighing at the empty cookie jar just so the whole room notices. That's the blank.

explanations.answer: Anoint your head and wash your face
explanations.explanation: Right. Jesus says, “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face…” (Matthew 6:17) It's the opposite of the hypocrites disfiguring their faces. The purpose He gives is “…so that your fasting will not be obvious to men…” (Matthew 6:18)

explanations.answer: Put ashes on your head and weep
explanations.explanation: That's not what Jesus says here, friend. He says, “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face…” (Matthew 6:17) Washing your face is a clean start, not a show.

explanations.answer: Tear your robe and cover your face
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say that. He says, “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face…” (Matthew 6:17) A washed face is a lot less dramatic than a torn robe.

explanations.answer: So your fasting isn't obvious to men
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Jesus gives. You anoint your head and wash your face “…so that your fasting will not be obvious to men, but only to your Father, who is unseen.” (Matthew 6:18) Men don't have to know. Your Father does.

explanations.answer: So you stay clean for the temple
explanations.explanation: The temple isn't part of this verse, friend. Jesus says to anoint your head and wash your face “…so that your fasting will not be obvious to men, but only to your Father, who is unseen.” (Matthew 6:17-18) The reason He gives is about who gets to see it.

explanations.answer: So you feel fresh while you go without
explanations.explanation: Feeling fresh sounds nice, but that isn't the reason in the text. Jesus gives this one: “…so that your fasting will not be obvious to men, but only to your Father, who is unseen.” (Matthew 6:18) The point is who gets to see it.
